catalog_quote: Kenyah languages, which also fall within WIn, have been described as having penultimate stress except where the penultimate vowel was schwa, in which case stress falls on the final syllable (Blust 2014; Blust 2007b via personal communication with Antonia Soriente). Identical patterns are found in other Western Indonesian languages in Borneo, including In Mukah Melanau where Blust (1988: 178) notes that stress occurs typically on the penultimate syllable in phrasal contexts but that stress occurs on the final syllable if the penultimate syllable has a schwa nucleus. Smith (2017a) also recorded final stress where the penultimate syllable contains a schwa in Sekapan. [...] 4.2.1 Type one: Gemination with stress shift after schwa. In some languages, a pattern of final-syllable onset gemination is observed, but stress does not regularize itself to the penultimate syllable. [...] In Sekapan, another Western Indonesian language of Borneo, final-syllable onsets automatically lengthen after a penultimate schwa, and stress is shifted to the final syllable (Smith 2017a). [...] (20) Sekapan (Smith 2017a) bəbaw [bəbːáw] 'tall' pətəbeə̯ [pətəbːéə̯] 'to meet' məjat [məjːát] 'to pull' məgəm [məgːə́m] 'strong'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sekapan word stress is regular and non-contrastive: it falls on the penultimate syllable (Smith 2022 Routledge ch., ex. 15: tanaʔ [ˈtanaʔ] 'land', paray [ˈparaj] 'rice'), but when the penult is an open syllable whose nucleus is schwa the onset of the final syllable geminates and stress shifts to the final syllable (bəbaw [bəbːáw], məjat [məjːát], pətəbeə̯ [pətəbːéə̯]). Smith analyses schwa as weightless (moraic account), so the pattern can also be read as weight-conditioned; there is no vowel-length contrast.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in Sekapan.
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate open-syllable schwa repels stress to the ultima (with gemination of the following onset); per Smith 2022 (Routledge Handbook, snippet) a schwa in a CLOSED penult can bear stress (nəkəp [nəˈkːəp] 'to lie prone', where the geminate closes the penult), and monosyllables such as dəm [ˈdːəm] 'dark' carry an initial geminate. Stress does not 'regularize' back to the penult after gemination (type-one language).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern citation forms of (mostly disyllabic) lexical words from Smith's own 2015-16 Belaga field data (Smith 2017a); no discussion of phrase-level prosody or affixed words.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Smith statements rest on his own Sekapan field data from the Sungai Panjang tributary of the Rejang near Belaga (consultants John Lupai and Singem Sirik; Smith 2017:1447ff), i.e. Sekapan proper = seka1248 [skp]. Strickland 1995 treats Kejaman and Sekapan as mutually intelligible varieties and Glottolog files it under Kajaman [kag]; the closely related Kejaman realises post-schwa gemination as a glottal-stop+C cluster (Smith 2017:4385), so Kejaman statements should not be transferred to Sekapan without note.

sources.note: Sec. 4.2.1 'Type one: Gemination with stress shift after schwa', p. [26] (p. 26), ex. (20): in Sekapan final-syllable onsets automatically lengthen after a penultimate schwa and stress is shifted to the final syllable; examples bəbaw [bəbːáw] 'tall', pətəbeə̯ [pətəbːéə̯] 'to meet', məjat [məjːát] 'to pull', məgəm [məgːə́m] 'strong' (data Smith 2017a = his own Belaga fieldwork). Type-one languages otherwise have penultimate stress that does not 'regularize' after gemination.
